what_its_for: Romosozumab-aqqg is used to treat osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) in women who have gone through menopause and are at high risk of breaking a bone. It works by both building new bone and slowing down bone loss at the same time, which helps make your bones stronger.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as two injections under the skin (subcutaneous injections) one right after the other, once a month. A healthcare provider will give you both shots during the same visit, usually in your stomach area (abdomen), upper arm, or thigh. You will NOT inject this medicine yourself at home. Each monthly treatment consists of two separate prefilled syringes given back-to-back.
dosing: The usual dose is 210 mg given once a month. This is made up of two injections of 105 mg each, given one right after the other at the same appointment. Treatment lasts for 12 months (12 monthly doses). After completing 12 months of treatment, your doctor will likely switch you to a different bone-strengthening medicine to continue protecting your bones.
missed_dose: If you miss or skip your monthly injection appointment, call your doctor or clinic as soon as possible to reschedule. Try to get your injection as soon as you can. After that, your next dose should be scheduled one month from the date of your rescheduled injection. Do not try to double up on doses.
storage: Romosozumab-aqqg is stored and handled by your healthcare provider or pharmacy. It must be kept in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). It should NOT be frozen. Keep it in the original carton to protect it from light. Before giving the injection, the medicine can be kept at room temperature (up to 77°F or 25°C) for up to 30 days. Once removed from the refrigerator and kept at room temperature, it must be used within 30 days or thrown away.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor if you have had a heart attack or stroke before, as this medicine may increase your risk of having another one. Avoid starting this medicine if your blood calcium levels are too low (hypocalcemia) — your doctor will check this before starting treatment. Make sure you are getting enough calcium and vitamin D while on this medicine; ask your doctor if you need supplements. Avoid missing your monthly injection appointments to get the full benefit of your treatment.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get emergency help right away if you experience: chest pain, shortness of breath, or sudden numbness or weakness on one side of your body (signs of a possible heart attack or stroke); jaw pain, swelling, or numbness, or loosening of teeth (possible jaw bone problems called osteonecrosis of the jaw); unusual thigh or groin pain that could be a sign of a rare thigh bone fracture; muscle cramps, numbness or tingling in your fingers or toes, or spasms around your mouth (signs of low calcium); skin redness, rash, itching, or swelling, especially of the face or throat (allergic reaction); or pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site that does not go away.
when_it_works: Romosozumab-aqqg starts building bone fairly quickly. Studies show it can significantly increase bone density and reduce the risk of fractures within the 12-month treatment period. However, you may not feel any different day to day because bone strengthening happens silently inside your body. Your doctor may order a bone density test (DEXA scan) to check how well the medicine is working. It is very important to continue the full 12 months of treatment and then follow up with another bone medicine as directed by your doctor.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): This medicine is commonly used in postmenopausal women and is generally appropriate for older women, but your doctor will carefully review your heart health before prescribing it. Kidney problems: If you have severe kidney disease or are on dialysis, you are at higher risk for low calcium levels. Your doctor will monitor your calcium closely. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: This medicine is only approved for use in postmenopausal women and should NOT be used during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Heart disease history: This medicine is NOT recommended if you have had a heart attack or stroke in the past year due to an increased risk of serious heart and blood vessel problems.
